title: Indian Economy
outcomes: Describe India's pre-colonial economy and the effects of British rule (1757–1947) on industry and agriculture.
Trace post-independence policy (planning, IPR 1948 and 1956, licence raj, Green Revolution, MRTP, SSI reservation) and explain the Hindu growth rate.
Explain the early reforms of the 1980s, the 1991 crisis, the objectives and measures of the 1991 reforms, and their outcomes using the growth table.
Explain the role and criticism of NITI Aayog and summarise the current state of the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors with the figures and years given in the study material.

meta.exam_tip: This chapter is fact-heavy. Learn each figure WITH its year exactly as the study material gives it (e.g. reserves US$1.2 billion in 1991; services 53.89% of GVA; NITI Aayog 1 January 2015; licensing except 18 → 5). Distinguish 1980s measures from 1991 measures.

concepts.title: Pre-colonial prosperity and the colonial economy (1757–1947)
body: Between the first and seventeenth centuries AD, India is believed to have been the largest economy in the world, holding between a third and a quarter of world wealth — self-reliant villages plus commercial and pilgrimage cities, and highly skilled artisans whose textiles and handicrafts sold worldwide.

Kautilya's Arthashastra (321–296 BCE) is the earliest known Indian treatise on economic thought and statecraft. "Artha" means material well-being, not just wealth; the text stresses productive agriculture, fair and easily understood taxes equal for private and state businesses, and a king who puts his people's good first. It names seven elements of the state: King, Ministers, Farmlands, Fortresses, Treasury, Military and Allies.

British rule: East India Company 1757–1858; British Crown 1858–1947. After Britain's industrial revolution, India was turned from an exporter of manufactures into an exporter of raw materials and a market for British machine-made goods. Discriminatory tariffs (heavy on Indian exports of finished goods, light on imports) and changing tastes destroyed Indian handicrafts — de-industrialisation.

Consequences: mass unemployment and crowding into agriculture; subdivision and fragmentation of holdings, subsistence farming, low productivity and poverty; the zamindari system creating a class loyal to British rule; high rents, absentee landlords, heavy indebtedness and exploitative moneylenders; near collapse of agriculture.

Modern industry grew from the mid-19th century — cotton mills and jute mills especially, plus brewing, paper, leather, matches and rice milling — but producer-goods industries lagged because British interests discouraged competing industries. Growth was too small to transform the economy.

blocks.title: Colonial-era industry in numbers

concepts.analogy: A master weaver forced to sell raw cotton cheaply and buy back factory cloth at a price he cannot compete with — that was India's trade position under colonial rule.
concepts.work: Economic history explains today's structure — small farms, a large informal sector, regional imbalance — that analysts and CAs must factor into credit, investment and policy analysis.

concepts.title: Post-independence strategy (1947–1991): planning, public sector, licence raj
body: At independence India was overwhelmingly rural, poor and deeply stratified; in 1951 literacy was just above 18% and life expectancy barely 32 years — poverty of human capital as well as income.

The Nehruvian model: state-directed industrialisation with redistribution; central planning through the Planning Commission and Five-Year Plans; "planned modernisation" with heavy industry as the cornerstone. Policies of the 1950s blended Nehru's socialist vision of heavy industry with Gandhian emphasis on small-scale and cottage industry and village republics.

Industrial Policy Resolution 1948: larger public-sector role and licensing for the private sector; state monopoly in atomic energy, arms and ammunition, and railways; new investment in basic industries reserved for the state. Industrial Policy Resolution 1956: a comprehensive framework but tilted heavily towards the public sector, dampening private enterprise.
Trade and investment were fairly open until the late 1950s; a balance-of-payments crisis in 1958 led to tighter import controls (kept until 1966) and curbs on licences needing imported capital goods.
1950–80: average GDP growth of a modest 3.5% — the "Hindu growth rate". The first decade and a half stressed capital goods — dams, power plants, heavy industry.

Controls multiplied: 14 banks nationalised in 1969 (6 more in 1980); the MRTP Act, 1969 restricted licensing, capacity expansion, mergers and acquisitions by large firms; from 1967 many products were reserved for small-scale units, keeping big firms out of labour-intensive industries where India could have competed globally; rigid labour laws added to this.

1965–81 was the worst period of independent India's economic history: licence raj, autarkic policies, three wars (1962, 1965, 1971), droughts (1966, 1967) and oil shocks (1973, 1979) — productivity fell and India, nearly closed, missed the boom in world trade. Equity-driven policies blunted the incentive to create wealth.
concepts.analogy: The licence raj was like needing a government permit to change the menu of your own restaurant — safe from competition, but slow, costly and stale.
concepts.work: Older companies' structures — conglomerates, captive units, legacy public-sector holdings — often trace back to this era's licensing and MRTP rules; understanding them helps in restructuring and valuation work.

concepts.title: The Green Revolution
body: Agriculture got less priority in the Second Plan, and the institutional approach (land reforms, cooperatives) without enough research and irrigation gave only modest gains.
Two consecutive severe droughts in 1966 and 1967 caused negative farm growth and a food crisis; India depended on US food aid under PL 480.

The policy shifted from institutional change to raising productivity, especially of wheat: high-yielding seed varieties with intensive use of water, fertilisers and pesticides — the Green Revolution. Food-grain output rose sharply and India overcame its food problem; by today the material describes India as a food-exporting nation and among the top ten exporters of agricultural products.
concepts.analogy: Instead of redistributing the same small cake (institutional reform), India learned to bake a much bigger one (technology).
concepts.work: Agri-input companies (seeds, fertilisers, pesticides, irrigation) and agri-lending still ride on Green Revolution technologies — sectors CAs audit and analyse.

concepts.title: Early liberalisation in the 1980s ("reforms by stealth")
body: From the early 1980s, and especially after 1985, tight money, fiscal moderation and selected structural reforms sought price stability and moved away from inward-looking trade and investment. These 1981–89 changes were ad hoc and little publicised — hence "reforms by stealth" — but growth improved: 5.7% in the Sixth Plan (1980–85) and 5.8% in the Seventh Plan (1985–90).

Measures (industry, trade, taxation, exchange rate): delicensing of 25 broad industry categories in 1985 (later more); "broad-banding" letting firms change product mix within existing capacity without a new licence (e.g. switching between trucks and cars); MRTP asset limit raised from ₹20 crore to ₹100 crore (1985-86); MODVAT replacing multipoint excise duties; SEBI set up as a non-statutory body on 12 April 1988; OGL list expanded (1,329 capital-goods items by April 1990); export incentives; a realistic exchange rate — real effective depreciation of about 30% from 1985-86 to 1989-90; decontrol of cement and aluminium; the 1986 budget cutting taxes, liberalising imports and reducing tariffs.

Limits: private investment still held back by licensing, public-sector reservations, SSI reservation and price controls; inefficient, low-return public sector; MRTP barriers; tariffs, quotas and bans on foreign investment insulating industry from competition.
Significance: they convinced policy makers that well-regulated competitive markets could deliver growth — laying the foundation for the systematic reforms of 1991.
concepts.analogy: The 1980s reforms were a trial run on a side road; 1991 was taking the whole economy onto the highway.
concepts.work: MODVAT was the ancestor of input tax credit — the same idea now central to GST compliance that CAs handle daily.

concepts.title: The 1991 crisis and the reform package (LPG)
body: Causes (Narasimha Rao government, 1991): revenue expenditure persistently above revenue receipts in the 1980s, deficits financed by domestic and external debt; swelling public debt and heavy interest payments; oil prices spiking with the 1990 Gulf war, straining the balance of payments; foreign exchange reserves down to just US$1.2 billion — about two weeks of imports — the immediate trigger; import squeeze cutting industrial output; dependence on IMF loans with strict conditions; and political fragility creating a "crisis of confidence". The collapse of the Soviet Union and China's outward-oriented success were lessons.

Two objectives: reorient a centrally directed, highly controlled economy towards a market-friendly one; and macroeconomic stabilisation through a big cut in the fiscal deficit. Measures were of two kinds — short-term stabilisation (inflation, balance of payments) and long-term structural reforms (productivity and competitiveness by removing rigidities). Popularly: liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation.

Fiscal reforms; monetary and financial-sector reforms (Narasimham Committee, 1991); SEBI made statutory (1992); the New Industrial Policy of 24 July 1991; and trade-policy reforms (dismantling quantitative restrictions, phased tariff cuts, removing import licensing, removing export duties, continuing export incentives).

blocks.title: The 1991 reform package at a glance

concepts.analogy: 1991 was like a patient in the emergency room: first stop the bleeding (stabilisation), then change the lifestyle (structural reform).
concepts.work: Almost every compliance area a CA handles today — SEBI regulation, FDI rules, bank prudential norms, current-account convertibility — was born or reshaped by the 1991 reforms.

concepts.title: Outcomes of three decades of reform
body: Broad results listed in the material (31 years of reform): deeper integration with the world economy; a market-oriented economy with far less government intervention; strong growth of private investment; world-class competitiveness in auto components, telecom, software, pharmaceuticals, biotechnology and professional services; easier access to foreign technology, inputs and finance; steady FDI and large portfolio inflows.

External strength: reserves close to eight months of import cover, among the largest in the world; a services trade surplus of around 3.7% of GDP thanks to IT and financial services; less pressure on the rupee than in other emerging market economies; a large domestic market sustaining demand; poverty reduced substantially; more competition and choice in banking and insurance; rapid infrastructure growth; a steadily falling share of agriculture in value added; a deeper financial sector.
Constraints: high fiscal deficit, inflation and debt — about 86% of GDP in FY21/22, above the 64.5% average for emerging market and developing economies in 2022 (IMF).

Growth record (Table 10.1, Economic Survey): growth fell to about 1.06% in the 1991 crisis year, mostly stayed between 4% and 8.5% thereafter, peaked at about 8.85% in 1999, dipped in 2008 (about 3.09%), contracted by about 6.60% in the pandemic year 2020 and rebounded to about 8.68% in 2021.
concepts.analogy: Three decades of reform gave India a bigger engine and a full fuel tank (reserves), but the vehicle still carries a heavy load of public debt.
concepts.work: Sovereign-risk analysis for investors and lenders weighs exactly these strengths (reserves, services surplus) against weaknesses (debt, deficits).

concepts.title: NITI Aayog
body: For nearly 64 years the Planning Commission drove public-investment-led planning. With a shift to market orientation, it was replaced on 1 January 2015 by the National Institution for Transforming India (NITI) Aayog — meant to spur innovative thinking by experts and promote co-operative federalism by giving states a bigger voice. It serves as the government's think tank and a "directional and policy dynamo".

Objectives (13 in all) include: a shared national vision with states; co-operative federalism ("strong states make a strong nation"); credible village-level plans aggregated upwards; national security in economic policy where referred; attention to groups at risk of being left behind; long-term strategic policy frameworks with monitoring; partnerships with think tanks and research institutions; a knowledge, innovation and entrepreneurship support system; a platform to resolve inter-sectoral and inter-departmental issues; a resource centre on good governance; monitoring and evaluation of programmes; technology upgradation and capacity building.

Key initiatives named in the material: LiFE (replacing the use-and-dispose economy), the National Data and Analytics Platform (NDAP), the Shoonya campaign (cleaner air through electric vehicles), E-Amrit (information portal on electric vehicles), India Policy Insights (IPI), the Methanol Economy programme (cut oil imports and emissions; convert coal and municipal waste into methanol) and a committee on Transforming India's Gold Market.

Criticism: a limited role — it does not make national plans, control spending or review state plans; above all it is excluded from the budget process; it lacks autonomy, and without the Planning Commission the Finance Ministry's short-term focus dominates, leaving no strong "voice of development".
concepts.analogy: The Planning Commission was the family elder who decided and funded everything; NITI Aayog is the family advisor who suggests, coordinates and tracks — but does not hold the purse.
concepts.work: NITI Aayog indices and reports (on states, innovation, data) are widely used by analysts and consultants for state-level and sector research.

concepts.title: Current state — primary sector (agriculture)
body: Agriculture and allied activities are India's largest source of livelihood. A food-deficit, import-dependent country until the late 1960s, India is now (per the material) number one in the world for milk, pulses, jute and spices; first in area sown to wheat, rice and cotton; number two for fruits, vegetables, tea, farmed fish, cotton, sugarcane, wheat, rice and sugar; has the largest cattle herd (buffaloes); and its food and grocery market is the sixth largest in the world, with retail making up 70% of sales. Livestock grew at a record 6.6% during 2010-19.

Figures given: about 47% of the population depends directly on agriculture; the sector's share in GVA was 18.8% in 2021-22; 2021-22 food-grain output: 315.7 million tonnes; private investment in agriculture: 9.3% (2020-21); index of agricultural production (2021-22, base TE 2007-08 = 100): above 140 for all crops, food-grains, cereals, wheat and coarse cereals, 138.7 for rice, 196.2 for pulses and 142.9 for non-food-grains; growth of 3.5% in 2022-23 (Economic Survey 2022-23). Agri exports reached an all-time high of ₹3,74,611 crore in the latest year noted; agri and processed food exports rose 25% in April–September 2022-23 over the same period a year earlier. APEDA promotes agri exports. Its share in GVA is falling but output keeps rising in absolute terms.

Support measures: MSP for all 23 mandated crops at 1.5 times the all-India weighted average cost of production; PM-KISAN income support; concessional institutional credit; National Mission for Edible Oils; PM Fasal Bima Yojana (crop insurance); MIDH (horticulture); Soil Health Cards; Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana (organic farming); Agriculture Infrastructure Fund; Farmer Producer Organisations; Per Drop More Crop and the Micro Irrigation Fund; mechanisation; e-NAM (online national market linking APMC mandis); Kisan Rail; agri start-ups; 100% FDI under the automatic route in marketing of food products and food-product e-commerce.

Problems: small, fragmented holdings and low productivity; resource-intensive, cereal-centric and regionally skewed farming straining water and soil; weak agro-processing and value chains; slow diversification and technology adoption; poor marketing, credit and warehousing; climate change and monsoon dependence; food-price volatility; unused export potential; poor post-harvest infrastructure; poverty and malnutrition.
concepts.analogy: Indian agriculture is a giant with weak legs — enormous output, but too many people on too little land with too little productivity.
concepts.work: Agri-credit, crop insurance, FPOs and commodity businesses form a big client base; knowing MSP, e-NAM and scheme design is useful for audit and advisory work in rural finance.

concepts.title: Current state — secondary sector (industry)
body: Industry contributes about 30% of GVA and employs over 12.1 crore people (per the material); the informal sector accounts for more than 50% of GVA. Manufacturing makes up 78% of industrial production; manufacturing GVA was estimated at US$77.47 billion in Q3 of 2021-22 and has contributed about 16.3% of nominal GVA over the past ten years. The eight-core-industries index was 142.8 for 2022-23 (up to September 2022); these eight industries (coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilisers, steel, cement, electricity) carry 40.27% of the weight in the IIP. Manufacturing PMI was 55.4 on 31 January 2023. DPIIT reported FDI inflows of US$58.77 billion in 2021-22.

Policies: GST from 1 July 2017 replacing many indirect taxes; optional 22% corporate tax for domestic companies forgoing exemptions; Make in India (2014; Make in India 2.0 covers 27 sectors — 15 manufacturing, 12 services); Ease of Doing Business — India 63rd in the World Bank's Doing Business Report 2020 against 77th in 2019 (14 places up); the National Single Window System; the PM Gati Shakti master plan for multimodal infrastructure; the National Logistics Policy (September 2022); PLI scheme (launched March 2020 for 14 key sectors, later extended to white goods); industrial corridors with plug-and-play infrastructure; FAME-India for electric and hybrid vehicles; Udyami Bharat for MSMEs; PM MITRA textile parks; FDI reforms (defence, pension, e-commerce; 100% automatic route for coal sale and mining and insurance intermediaries); FIPB scrapped in May 2017, its place taken by the Foreign Investment Facilitation Portal (853 proposals disposed of in 5 years; FDI up 39% since); RoDTEP (2021) replacing MEIS; Start-up India; Public Procurement (Preference to Make in India) Order, 2017; Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme. Global Innovation Index rank improved from 81st (2015) to 40th (2022). The National Manufacturing Policy aims at 25% of GDP from manufacturing by 2025; Industry 4.0 is the next frontier.

Challenges: weak infrastructure and skills; import dependence and exchange-rate risk; poor credit access for MSMEs; badly located units; loss-making public enterprises; labour disputes; weak export competitiveness and foreign NTBs; supply-chain disruption; inflation and input costs; global slowdown; monetary tightening; high fuel prices; a growing informal sector.
concepts.analogy: Industry is India's middle floor — sturdy but never fully built; policy now tries to add the missing storeys.
concepts.work: PLI claims, GST, RoDTEP and FDI filings are routine CA work in manufacturing companies; knowing the policy landscape is directly billable knowledge.

concepts.title: Current state — tertiary sector (services) and conclusion
body: India's unusual path: growth moved from agriculture straight to services, largely bypassing the usual shift to industry.

Services (the 15 groups of the National Industrial Classification 2008 include trade, transport, accommodation and food, information and communication, finance and insurance, real estate, professional and technical services, administration, public administration and defence, education, health, arts and entertainment, household activities and extra-territorial bodies) form the largest sector: 53.89% of GVA, with services GVA at current prices estimated at ₹96.54 lakh crore in 2020-21 (per the material). It is the fastest-growing sector with the highest labour productivity, powered by knowledge-based and IT-enabled services; most start-ups are in services.

Trade and investment: India is among the top 10 WTO members in services exports and imports; services exports were US$27.0 billion in November 2022 and stayed resilient through the pandemic. Services are the largest recipient of FDI — more than 60% of FDI equity inflows. UNCTAD's World Investment Report 2022 ranks India 7th among the top 20 FDI host countries for 2021. For 2021-22 the material reports record FDI inflows of US$84.8 billion, of which FDI equity into services was US$7.1 billion. 100% FDI is allowed in telecom services through the automatic route; the FDI cap in insurance was raised from 49% to 74%.

Conclusion (World Bank, India Development Update, November 2022): despite the Russia–Ukraine war, high commodity prices, supply disruptions, tighter finance and domestic inflation, India's real GDP grew 6.3% in July–September 2022-23 on strong private consumption and investment; its large domestic market makes it more insulated from global spill-overs and more resilient than other emerging markets.
concepts.analogy: India skipped a rung on the development ladder — from the farm straight to the office — which makes it strong in services but leaves the factory floor under-filled.
concepts.work: CAs themselves are part of this sector; IT, financial and professional services exports (including accounting outsourcing) are a growth area for Indian firms and practitioners.

illustrations.title: What the post-1991 growth table tells us
illustrations.q: Using the GDP growth table in the study material (annual %, 1991–2021, source: Economic Survey), compute (a) the average growth for 1992–1996, 2003–2007 and 2017–2021, (b) the average for the whole period 1991–2021, (c) the swing between 2020 and 2021. Compare with the "Hindu growth rate" of 3.5% (1950–80). Which year had the highest growth and which the lowest?

head: Year
GDP growth (%) — selected years, rounded
given.title: Extract (full table used in the working)

solution.text: Every period average after 1991 is well above the 3.5% Hindu growth rate. Highest single year: 1999 (8.85%); lowest: 2020 (-6.6%, the pandemic year), followed by a sharp rebound in 2021 (8.68%). Low years such as 1991 (1.06%, the crisis year) and 2008 (3.09%, the global financial crisis) show the effect of shocks.

illustrations.title: Putting numbers on the reform story
illustrations.q: From the study material: the highest tariff was 355% in 1990-91, 85% in 1993-94, 50% in 1995-96 and 10% by 2007-08 (with exceptions); the MRTP asset limit was raised from ₹20 crore to ₹100 crore in 1985-86; 14 banks were nationalised in 1969 and 6 more in 1980; GDP grew on average 5.7% in the Sixth Plan and 5.8% in the Seventh Plan. Compute (a) the fall in the top tariff from 1990-91 to 1993-94 in percentage points and in relative terms, and the relative fall up to 2007-08; (b) the change in the MRTP limit; (c) total banks nationalised; (d) how far the 1980s plan growth exceeded the Hindu growth rate.

solution.text: Distinguish "percentage points" (simple difference between two rates) from "per cent" (relative change). A cut from 355% to 85% is 270 percentage points, i.e. about 76% of the original rate.

illustrations.title: How thin was the cushion in 1991?
illustrations.q: The study material says that in 1991 India's foreign exchange reserves fell to only US$1.2 billion, barely enough for two weeks of imports. Roughly what weekly and annual import bill does this imply? Compare with the post-reform position the material describes.

solution.text: By contrast, the material notes that India now holds reserves close to eight months of import cover and one of the largest stocks of international reserves in the world.
The weekly and annual figures are rough inferences from "two weeks of imports"; the exam fact to remember is US$1.2 billion ≈ two weeks of imports (1991).

jobs.title: Sector note for an equity research report
jobs.role: Research analyst at a broking firm
jobs.situation: You are writing the macro section of an initiation report on an Indian manufacturing company and must quote official data.
steps: Use the official source and state the period for every figure (e.g. manufacturing PMI, core-industries index, FDI inflows).
Show trends with the growth table and highlight shock years (1991, 2008, 2020).
Link company prospects to policies (PLI, Make in India, National Logistics Policy, GST).
Flag risks named in policy documents — input costs, monetary tightening, global slowdown.
jobs.takeaway: Macro numbers are only credible with the source and year attached — the same discipline the exam expects.

jobs.takeaway: Knowing the scheme landscape lets a CA turn policy into cash flow for rural clients.

mcqs.q: Between the 1st and 17th centuries AD, India is believed to have controlled roughly what share of world wealth?
mcqs.explain: According to the study material, India was probably the world's biggest economy from the 1st to the 17th century AD, holding between one-third and one-fourth of global wealth, thanks to skilled artisans and textiles. 'More than half' is the trap — an exaggeration; 'about 2%' is closer to India's share at independence. In practice: economic historians use this contrast to show how colonial rule reversed India's prosperity.
mcqs.topic: Status of Indian Economy: Pre Independence Period (1850 -1947)

mcqs.q: The Arthashastra is attributed to:
mcqs.explain: The Arthashastra, the earliest known Indian treatise on economic philosophy and statecraft, is attributed to Kautilya, also called Chanakya (around 321–296 BCE). Chandragupta Maurya is the trap: the text is believed to have been a handbook written for him, not by him. In practice: modern Indian public-finance writers still quote Kautilya's ideas on fair, easily understood taxation.
mcqs.topic: Status of Indian Economy: Pre Independence Period (1850 -1947)

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the seven elements of the state in the Arthashastra?
mcqs.explain: The Arthashastra lists seven elements of the state: the king, ministers, farmlands (territory), fortresses, treasury, military and allies. A Parliament is a modern democratic institution, not part of Kautilya's framework. 'Allies' is tempting to reject because it sounds like foreign policy, but it is one of the seven. In practice: management writers in India often adapt this seven-element model to discuss organisational strength.
mcqs.topic: Status of Indian Economy: Pre Independence Period (1850 -1947)

mcqs.q: The rule of the East India Company in India lasted from:
mcqs.explain: The material divides colonial rule into two phases: East India Company rule from 1757 (after the Battle of Plassey) to 1858, and British Crown rule from 1858 to 1947. '1858 to 1947' is the trap — that is Crown rule, which began after the 1857 revolt. In practice: historians trace the start of India's de-industrialisation to the Company period's trade and revenue policies.
mcqs.topic: Status of Indian Economy: Pre Independence Period (1850 -1947)

mcqs.q: The colonial policy of discriminatory tariffs meant:
options: Heavy duties on Indian exports of finished goods and low duties on British imports
mcqs.explain: Under discriminatory tariffs, the British charged heavy duties on Indian exports of finished goods and low duties on British manufactured imports into India, making Indian manufactures uncompetitive at home and abroad. 'Free trade on equal terms' is the trap — the policy was deliberately one-sided. In practice: this history explains why post-independence planners initially favoured protection for domestic industry.
mcqs.topic: Status of Indian Economy: Pre Independence Period (1850 -1947)

mcqs.q: According to the material, in the 1930s India ranked ___ in the world in number of cotton spindles.
mcqs.explain: Per the material, India's cotton mill industry had 9 million spindles in the 1930s, placing it fifth in the world. Eighth is the trap — that was the rank of India's iron industry by output in 1930; twelfth was India's rank as an industrialised country before the Great Depression. In practice: the cotton textile base later helped centres such as Mumbai and Ahmedabad become major industrial hubs.
mcqs.topic: Status of Indian Economy: Pre Independence Period (1850 -1947)

mcqs.q: Leaving out small-scale and cottage units, manufacturing's share in India's NDP in 1946 was barely about:
mcqs.explain: The material states that factory manufacturing (leaving out small-scale and cottage units) contributed only about 7% of net domestic product as late as 1946 — evidence of limited industrialisation under colonial rule. The tempting 1.4% is a different statistic: factory employment as a share of population in 1941. In practice: economic historians cite these figures to show how little structural change took place before 1947.
mcqs.topic: Status of Indian Economy: Pre Independence Period (1850 -1947)

mcqs.q: In 1951, India's literacy rate was just above ___ and life expectancy barely ___ years.
mcqs.explain: Per the material, in 1951 India's literacy rate was just above 18% and life expectancy barely 32 years, so poverty was in human capability as well as income. The trap '32%; 18' swaps the two numbers. In practice: these figures explain why the early Five-Year Plans emphasised education and health, and why human-development indicators are tracked in every Economic Survey today.

mcqs.q: The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1948 granted state monopoly in:
options: Atomic energy, arms and ammunition, and railways
mcqs.explain: The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1948 gave the state a monopoly in strategic areas — atomic energy, arms and ammunition, and railways — and reserved new investment in basic industries for the state. 'Banking and insurance' is the trap: banks were nationalised much later, in 1969 and 1980, and insurance in 1956 and 1972. In practice: railways and atomic energy remain largely state-run even today.

mcqs.q: The average annual GDP growth of about 3.5% during 1950–80 is called the:
mcqs.explain: The modest average GDP growth of about 3.5% a year from 1950 to 1980, under a controlled, inward-looking regime, came to be called the 'Hindu growth rate'. 'Plan growth rate' is the trap — it is not the established term. In practice: economists compare this rate with growth of 6–8% after the 1991 reforms to argue that liberalisation lifted India's growth potential.

mcqs.q: A balance-of-payments crisis that led to tighter import controls emerged in:
mcqs.explain: The material notes that a balance-of-payments crisis emerged in 1958, raising concerns about foreign exchange and leading to tighter import controls, which were maintained comprehensively until 1966. 1966 is the trap — that is when the controls began to ease, not when the crisis started; 1991 is the later, bigger crisis. In practice: India's repeated foreign-exchange crises are why RBI today keeps large reserves.

mcqs.q: How many banks were nationalised in 1969?
mcqs.explain: The government nationalised 14 major banks in 1969 and another 6 in 1980, making 20 in all. The trap 20 is the combined total, and 6 is the 1980 batch. In practice: public sector banks such as SBI and Bank of Baroda still hold a large share of Indian deposits, a legacy of nationalisation that CAs encounter in bank audits.

mcqs.q: The MRTP Act was enacted in:
mcqs.explain: The Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act was enacted in 1969 to regulate large firms, requiring approvals for licensing, expansion, mergers and acquisitions. 1991 is the trap — that is when the Act was restructured and its merger provisions repealed. In practice: the Competition Act, 2002 later replaced the MRTP framework, moving from controlling size to curbing anti-competitive behaviour.

mcqs.q: The policy of reserving products for exclusive manufacture by the small-scale sector began in:
mcqs.explain: From 1967, India reserved a long list of products to be made only by small-scale units, keeping large firms out of labour-intensive industries. 1956 is the trap — that year saw the Industrial Policy Resolution expanding the public sector. In practice: de-reservation after 1991 allowed large firms to enter areas such as garments and toys, a change economists credit with improving scale and exports.

mcqs.q: According to the material, the worst period of economic performance in independent India was:
mcqs.explain: The material describes 1965–81 as the worst period of economic performance in independent India — licence raj, autarky, three wars (1962, 1965 and 1971), major droughts in 1966 and 1967, and oil shocks. 1981–91 is the trap: growth actually improved then under early liberalisation. In practice: this period is the standard case study for why heavy controls slowed India's growth.

mcqs.q: The Green Revolution was triggered mainly by:
options: Severe droughts in 1966 and 1967 and the resulting food crisis
mcqs.explain: Severe droughts in 1966 and 1967 cut farm output sharply, and India had to rely on US food aid under PL 480. This crisis pushed the government towards the Green Revolution strategy. The 1991 crisis is the trap — it triggered industrial and trade reforms, not the Green Revolution. In practice: India's food self-sufficiency today, with large FCI stocks, traces back to this response.

mcqs.q: The Green Revolution relied mainly on:
options: High-yielding seeds with intensive use of water, fertilisers and pesticides
mcqs.explain: The Green Revolution relied on high-yielding seed varieties together with intensive use of water, fertilisers and pesticides — a shift from an institutional strategy (land reform, cooperatives) to a technological one, especially for wheat. 'Land reforms and cooperatives' is the trap — that was the earlier approach. In practice: Punjab and Haryana's high wheat yields, and their groundwater and soil concerns, are legacies of this strategy.

mcqs.q: The 1981–89 liberalisation is often called:
mcqs.explain: The liberalisation of 1981–89 is called 'reforms by stealth' because it was ad hoc and not widely publicised, unlike the declared 1991 package. 'Big-bang reforms' is the trap — that describes the comprehensive changes of 1991. In practice: economists credit these quieter reforms with lifting growth in the 1980s, setting the stage for the bigger changes that followed.

mcqs.q: Average annual GDP growth in the Sixth Plan (1980–85) and Seventh Plan (1985–90) was respectively:
mcqs.explain: Per the material, average annual GDP growth was 5.7% during the Sixth Plan (1980–85) and 5.8% during the Seventh Plan (1985–90), well above the 3.5% of earlier decades. The trap '5.8% and 5.7%' reverses the order; '3.5% and 3.5%' is the Hindu growth rate of 1950–80. In practice: this improvement is evidence that early liberalisation helped growth even before 1991.

mcqs.q: "Broad-banding" in the 1980s allowed firms to:
options: Change their product mix within existing capacity without a fresh licence
mcqs.explain: Broad-banding, introduced in the 1980s, let firms in an industry group change their product mix within existing licensed capacity without a fresh licence — for example, switching between trucks and cars. 'Import consumer goods freely' is the trap: imports stayed restricted then. In practice: this flexibility helped automobile and engineering firms respond to demand, a small step towards the later abolition of licensing.

mcqs.q: In 1985-86, the asset limit for MRTP firms was raised from ₹20 crore to ₹100 crore. By how many times did it increase?
mcqs.explain: The asset limit rose from ₹20 crore to ₹100 crore: 100 ÷ 20 = 5 times. The tempting 4 times confuses the increase of 400% (an extra 80 crore over 20) with the multiple; 80 is the rupee increase, not times. In practice: raising such thresholds let more mid-sized firms grow without MRTP approvals — a common reform tool, similar to how MSME definitions are revised today.

mcqs.q: SEBI was first set up as a non-statutory body on:
mcqs.explain: SEBI was set up as a non-statutory body on 12 April 1988 by a government resolution, and it received statutory powers in 1992 under the SEBI Act. 24 July 1991 is the trap — that is the date of the New Industrial Policy. In practice: CAs dealing with listed companies work within SEBI's LODR and ICDR regulations, issued under the powers SEBI gained in 1992.

mcqs.q: Based on REER, the rupee was depreciated from 1985-86 to 1989-90 by about:
mcqs.explain: The material notes that, measured by the real effective exchange rate, the rupee was depreciated by about 30% between 1985-86 and 1989-90, showing a changed official attitude towards exchange-rate adjustment. 18% is the trap — that refers to the July 1991 devaluation. In practice: exporters gained competitiveness from this real depreciation, which economists link to better export growth in the late 1980s.

mcqs.q: In 1991, India's foreign exchange reserves had fallen to about:
options: US$1.2 billion — barely two weeks of imports
US$12 billion — two months of imports
US$1.2 billion — eight months of imports
mcqs.explain: In 1991, India's foreign-exchange reserves fell to about US$1.2 billion, barely enough for two weeks of imports — the immediate trigger for the reforms. 'US$1.2 billion — eight months of imports' is the trap: eight months of import cover describes the much stronger post-reform position. In practice: this crisis, when India pledged gold to raise funds, is why RBI now maintains large reserves.

mcqs.q: The twin objectives of the 1991 reforms were:
options: A market-oriented economy and macroeconomic stabilisation by cutting the fiscal deficit
Fixed exchange rate and higher tariffs
Bigger public sector and more licensing
mcqs.explain: The 1991 reforms had twin objectives: reorienting the economy towards markets and stabilising the macroeconomy by cutting the fiscal deficit. 'Nationalisation and import substitution' is the trap — those were features of the pre-1991 strategy the reforms moved away from. In practice: fiscal deficit targets and market-friendly policies in today's Union Budgets continue these twin themes.

mcqs.q: Short-term measures aimed at inflation and the adverse balance of payments in 1991 are called:
mcqs.explain: Stabilisation measures are short-term steps to control inflation and correct the adverse balance of payments, such as fiscal tightening. 'Structural reforms' is the trap: they are long-term, continuing changes such as delicensing and trade liberalisation. In practice: economists distinguish the 1991 stabilisation package, which addressed the immediate crisis, from the structural reforms that reshaped India over the following decades.

mcqs.q: The New Industrial Policy was announced on:
mcqs.explain: The New Industrial Policy was announced on 24 July 1991 and largely ended the licence raj by abolishing industrial licensing for most industries. 12 April 1988 is the trap — that is when SEBI was set up as a non-statutory body; 1 January 2015 is when NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission. In practice: Indian business histories mark 24 July 1991, also Budget day that year, as the start of modern liberalisation.

mcqs.q: Under the New Industrial Policy, licensing was abolished for all industries except:
mcqs.explain: The 1991 policy abolished licensing for all industries except 18, kept for security, strategic, social, safety and environmental reasons; the list was later cut to 5. The tempting 8 is the number of industries initially reserved for the public sector; 5 is today's licensing list. In practice: CAs advising on new manufacturing projects check whether the product falls in the remaining licensed industries.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT among the industries that, as per the material, still need a licence?
options: Distillation and brewing of alcoholic drinks
mcqs.explain: Per the material, only five industries now need a licence — arms and ammunition; atomic substances; narcotics and hazardous chemicals; alcoholic drinks; and cigarettes and cigars. Steel is not on the list. Cigarettes are a tempting distractor, but they do need a licence because of health concerns. In practice: steel companies can expand capacity without an industrial licence, subject to environmental clearances.

mcqs.q: Industries now reserved for the public sector (as per the material) are:
mcqs.explain: After 1991, the public sector's reserved list shrank from eight industries to only two: parts of atomic energy and core railway transport activities. 'Coal and steel' is the trap — they were opened to private players. Banking and insurance also allow private firms. In practice: private companies now operate coal mines, steel plants and airlines, while railway operations and nuclear power remain largely state-run.

mcqs.q: The 1991 policy introduced automatic approval for FDI up to:
mcqs.explain: The 1991 policy introduced automatic approval for foreign direct investment up to 51%, later extended to nearly all industries. 74% is the trap — it is a later cap in sectors such as insurance (from 2021) and some defence investment, not the 1991 threshold. In practice: today most sectors allow 100% FDI under the automatic route, and CAs file the related FEMA reports with RBI.

mcqs.q: According to the material, FDI is prohibited in:
options: Retail trade, atomic energy, lottery, and betting and gambling
mcqs.explain: Per the study material, FDI is barred in four sectors — retail trade, atomic energy, lotteries, and betting or gambling. 'Insurance and telecom' is the trap — both allow substantial FDI. Note that under current policy retail is partly open (single-brand retail up to 100%), but exam answers should follow the material. In practice: CAs check the latest consolidated FDI policy before advising foreign clients.

mcqs.q: The highest tariff rate of 355% in 1990-91 was reduced to 85% in 1993-94. The cut in percentage points is:
mcqs.explain: Fall in percentage points = 355 − 85 = 270 percentage points. The tempting 76.06 is the relative cut in percent: (355 − 85) ÷ 355 × 100. 85 is the new rate itself; 305 is an arithmetic slip. In practice: trade economists distinguish percentage-point changes from percentage changes when describing tariff cuts — a frequent confusion in budget commentaries.

mcqs.q: In July 1991 the rupee was devalued against the dollar by about:
mcqs.explain: In July 1991, India devalued the rupee against the dollar by between 18% and 19% under its then-fixed exchange-rate system. 30% is the trap — that was the real depreciation of 1985-86 to 1989-90. In practice: this devaluation, together with tariff cuts, made Indian exports more competitive and is cited in every account of the 1991 crisis response.

mcqs.q: India unified its exchange rate and allowed the rupee to float for the first time in:
mcqs.explain: India moved to a dual exchange rate in March 1992 and unified the rate in March 1993, allowing the rupee to float for the first time; since then it has followed a managed float. March 1992 is the trap — that introduced the dual-rate system, not the float. In practice: RBI intervenes in the forex market to smooth volatility, which is how India's managed float operates today.

mcqs.q: The government's agreement with the RBI (September 1994) aimed to:
options: Phase out deficit financing by money creation by 1997-98
mcqs.explain: Under a historic agreement in September 1994, the government and RBI agreed to phase out the automatic financing of deficits by money creation (ad hoc treasury bills) by 1997-98. 'Raise CRR' is the trap — it is a monetary tool unrelated to this agreement. In practice: ending automatic monetisation strengthened RBI's control over money supply, a foundation for today's inflation-targeting framework.

mcqs.q: Reduction of CRR and SLR and prudential norms for banks followed the recommendations of the:
mcqs.explain: Cuts in CRR and SLR, along with prudential norms on income recognition, asset classification and provisioning for banks, followed the Narasimham Committee's recommendations of 1991. 'NITI Aayog' is the trap — it was created only in 2015. In practice: bank auditors apply RBI's income-recognition and asset-classification (IRAC) norms, which trace back to these reforms.

mcqs.q: As per the material, India's public debt in FY21/22 was about ___ of GDP, against an EMDE average of 64.5% (2022).
mcqs.explain: Per the material, India's public debt was about 86% of GDP in FY21/22, higher than the 64.5% average for emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs) in 2022 (IMF). The tempting 64.5% is the EMDE average, not India's figure. In practice: rating agencies cite India's high debt ratio as a key constraint on its sovereign rating, so fiscal consolidation features in every Budget.

mcqs.q: Post-reform foreign exchange reserves, as per the material, provide import cover of close to:
mcqs.explain: Post-reform, the material notes that India's foreign-exchange reserves can pay for nearly eight months of imports. 'Two weeks' is the trap — that was the crisis position of 1991. In practice: this strong reserve cushion gives RBI room to curb rupee volatility and reassures foreign investors and rating agencies.

mcqs.q: According to Table 10.1 (Economic Survey), in which year did India record the highest GDP growth between 1991 and 2021?
mcqs.explain: Per Table 10.1 in the material, growth peaked at about 8.85% in 1999, the highest between 1991 and 2021. Close contenders are traps: 2021 at about 8.68%, 2010 at about 8.50% and 2016 at about 8.26%. In practice: analysts must read growth tables carefully, since several years cluster near 8–9% and rounding can change the ranking.

mcqs.q: According to Table 10.1, India's GDP growth in 2020 was about:
mcqs.explain: Per Table 10.1 in the material, India's GDP shrank by about 6.6% in 2020 because of the Covid-19 pandemic and lockdowns. The tempting 3.74% is 2019's growth; 8.68% is 2021's rebound; −1.06% reverses the sign of 1991's 1.06% growth. In practice: companies and auditors treated 2020 as an exceptional year when assessing going concern, impairment and loan moratoria.

mcqs.q: NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on:
mcqs.explain: On 1 January 2015, the National Institution for Transforming India (NITI) Aayog replaced the Planning Commission, which had functioned since 1950. 24 July 1991 is the trap — that is the New Industrial Policy date; 1 July 2017 is when GST began. In practice: NITI Aayog now publishes indices such as the SDG India Index and Export Preparedness Index, which policymakers and consultants use.
mcqs.topic: NITI Aayog: a Bold Step for Transforming India

mcqs.q: NITI Aayog is primarily meant to act as:
options: A think tank promoting co-operative federalism
The body that allocates central funds to states
The authority that approves the Union budget
mcqs.explain: NITI Aayog serves as the government's think tank and policy adviser, promoting co-operative federalism by giving States a stronger voice. 'The body that allocates central funds to states' is the trap — unlike the Planning Commission, it has no role in allocating funds. In practice: NITI Aayog's role is advisory, such as designing strategies for electric mobility or reviewing State performance indices.
mcqs.topic: NITI Aayog: a Bold Step for Transforming India

mcqs.q: The major shortcoming of NITI Aayog pointed out by critics is:
options: Its exclusion from the budgeting process
Too much control over state plans
mcqs.explain: Critics point out that NITI Aayog is excluded from the budgeting process: it does not make national plans, control spending or review State plans as the Planning Commission did. 'Excessive spending powers' is the trap — it actually has none. In practice: budget allocations to ministries and States are handled by the Finance Ministry and the Finance Commission, not NITI Aayog.
mcqs.topic: NITI Aayog: a Bold Step for Transforming India

mcqs.q: Which NITI Aayog initiative aims to cut the oil import bill by converting coal and municipal waste into a fuel?
mcqs.explain: NITI Aayog's Methanol Economy programme aims to cut India's oil import bill and emissions by converting coal reserves and municipal solid waste into methanol fuel. Shoonya is the trap — it promotes zero-pollution delivery vehicles; E-Amrit is an information portal on electric vehicles; NDAP is a data platform. In practice: methanol blending in petrol is being explored as part of India's energy-security strategy.
mcqs.topic: NITI Aayog: a Bold Step for Transforming India

mcqs.q: As per the material, India is the world's largest producer of:
mcqs.explain: Per the material, India leads the world in producing milk, pulses, jute and spices, and second-largest in items such as fruits, vegetables, tea, farmed fish, cotton, sugarcane, wheat, rice and sugar. 'Wheat and rice' is the trap — India is second in those, after China. In practice: dairy cooperatives such as Amul are central to India's leading position in milk production.
mcqs.topic: The Current State of the Indian Economy: a Brief Overview

mcqs.q: According to the material, about what share of India's population depends directly on agriculture?
mcqs.explain: Per the material, about 47% of India's population depends directly on agriculture for its livelihood. 18.8% is the trap — that is agriculture's share in gross value added in 2021-22, showing low productivity per worker. 53.89% is the services share of GVA. In practice: this gap is why policy focuses on farm incomes and moving workers into manufacturing and services.
mcqs.topic: The Current State of the Indian Economy: a Brief Overview

mcqs.q: Food-grain production in 2021-22, as per the material, reached:
mcqs.explain: Per the material, India's food-grain production reached 315.7 million tonnes in 2021-22. The other figures are traps from the same chapter: 196.2 is the production index for pulses and 142.8 the index of eight core industries. In practice: record food-grain output supports the PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana and keeps FCI stocks high.
mcqs.topic: The Current State of the Indian Economy: a Brief Overview

mcqs.q: MSP for the 23 mandated crops is fixed at:
options: 1.5 times the all-India weighted average cost of production
mcqs.explain: Per the material, MSP for each of the 23 mandated crops is set at one and a half times the all-India weighted average cost of production. 'Equal to cost of production' is the trap — that would give farmers no margin. In practice: the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP) recommends MSPs each season, and government procurement at MSP supports farm incomes.
mcqs.topic: The Current State of the Indian Economy: a Brief Overview

mcqs.q: A pan-India electronic trading portal linking APMC mandis into a unified national market is:
mcqs.explain: e-NAM is a pan-India electronic trading portal that links existing APMC mandis into a unified national market for farm commodities, improving price discovery. PM-KISAN is the trap — it provides direct income support to farmers. PMFBY is crop insurance and APEDA promotes farm exports. In practice: traders and farmer producer organisations use e-NAM to bid across mandis online.
mcqs.topic: The Current State of the Indian Economy: a Brief Overview

mcqs.q: Industry's contribution to India's GVA, as per the material, is about:
mcqs.explain: Per the material, the industrial sector contributes about 30% of India's total gross value added. 53.89% is the trap — that is the services sector's share; 18.8% is agriculture's. In practice: the government's aim, through schemes such as PLI and Make in India, is to raise manufacturing's share and create more industrial jobs.
mcqs.topic: The Current State of the Indian Economy: a Brief Overview

mcqs.q: The eight core industries carry what weight in the Index of Industrial Production?
mcqs.explain: Per the material, the eight core industries — coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilisers, steel, cement and electricity — carry 40.27% of the weight in the Index of Industrial Production. 55.4 is the trap: it was the manufacturing PMI on 31 January 2023. In practice: economists read the monthly core-industries index as an early signal of the IIP.
mcqs.topic: The Current State of the Indian Economy: a Brief Overview

mcqs.q: GST was introduced on:
mcqs.explain: GST was introduced on 1 July 2017, replacing central excise, service tax, State VAT and several other indirect taxes with a single destination-based tax. 1 April 2017 is the trap — the start of a financial year, but GST came three months later. In practice: CAs file GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B returns and conduct GST audits for clients under this regime.
mcqs.topic: The Current State of the Indian Economy: a Brief Overview

mcqs.q: When it began in March 2020, the PLI scheme covered how many key sectors?
mcqs.explain: Per the material, the Production Linked Incentive scheme began in March 2020 for 14 key sectors, to boost manufacturing and exports. 27 is the trap — that is the number of sectors under Make in India 2.0; 23 is the number of MSP crops. In practice: companies claiming PLI incentives need CA certification of incremental sales and investment.
mcqs.topic: The Current State of the Indian Economy: a Brief Overview

mcqs.q: India's rank in the World Bank's Doing Business Report 2020 was:
mcqs.explain: Per the material, India ranked 63rd in the World Bank's Doing Business Report 2020, up 14 places from 77th in 2019. 77th is the trap — the 2019 rank. 40th and 81st are India's Global Innovation Index ranks for 2022 and 2015. In practice: the World Bank discontinued the Doing Business report in 2021, so investors now rely on other indicators.
mcqs.topic: The Current State of the Indian Economy: a Brief Overview

mcqs.q: After the FIPB was scrapped in May 2017, FDI approvals moved to:
mcqs.explain: After the Foreign Investment Promotion Board was abolished in May 2017, FDI approvals moved to the Foreign Investment Facilitation Portal, which routes proposals to the relevant ministries. The National Single Window System is the trap — it is a broader investor-approval platform, not the FIPB's replacement. In practice: CAs file government-route FDI applications through this portal.
mcqs.topic: The Current State of the Indian Economy: a Brief Overview

mcqs.q: RoDTEP (2021) replaced which export scheme?
mcqs.explain: RoDTEP (Remission of Duties and Taxes on Export Products), launched in 2021, replaced the Merchandise Exports from India Scheme (MEIS). It refunds hidden central, State and local levies on exported goods not refunded elsewhere. PLI is the trap — it is a production incentive, not an export-duty remission scheme. In practice: exporters' CAs track RoDTEP credits on shipping bills.
mcqs.topic: The Current State of the Indian Economy: a Brief Overview

mcqs.q: India's distinctive growth path, as per the material, was a shift:
options: From agriculture directly to services, largely bypassing industry
From agriculture to industry and then to services
mcqs.explain: Unlike the usual path of agriculture to industry to services, India shifted largely from agriculture straight to services, largely skipping the industrial stage. 'From agriculture to industry and then to services' is the trap — that is the sequence followed by most developed economies. In practice: India's IT and services boom alongside a smaller manufacturing share explains policy efforts like Make in India.
mcqs.topic: The Current State of the Indian Economy: a Brief Overview

mcqs.q: The services sector's share of India's total GVA, as per the material, is:
mcqs.explain: Per the material, services account for 53.89% of India's total GVA, making it the largest sector. 30% is the trap — industry's share; 18.8% is agriculture's. In practice: services such as IT, finance, trade and telecom dominate India's output and exports, and many CAs work in this sector in finance, audit and advisory roles.
mcqs.topic: The Current State of the Indian Economy: a Brief Overview

mcqs.q: FDI equity inflows into services account for what share of total FDI equity inflows into India (per the material)?
mcqs.explain: Per the material, the services sector received more than 60% of total FDI equity inflows into India, making it the largest recipient. 'About 30%' is the trap — it echoes industry's share of GVA, a different statistic. In practice: sectors such as computer software, financial services and trading attract the bulk of FDI, which CAs see when handling FEMA reporting for clients.
mcqs.topic: The Current State of the Indian Economy: a Brief Overview

mcqs.q: The FDI cap in insurance companies was raised from:
mcqs.explain: Per the material, the FDI cap in insurance companies was raised from 49% to 74% (a change made in 2021). '26% to 49%' is the trap — that was the earlier increase, made in 2015. Telecom services now allow 100% FDI under the automatic route. In practice: the higher cap let foreign insurers raise stakes in Indian joint ventures, and CAs advise on the valuation and FEMA aspects.
mcqs.topic: The Current State of the Indian Economy: a Brief Overview

mcqs.q: The World Bank's India Development Update (November 2022) noted that India's real GDP grew by ___ in July–September 2022-23.
mcqs.explain: Per the material, the World Bank's India Development Update of November 2022 noted that India's real GDP grew by 6.3% in July–September 2022-23, driven by strong private consumption and investment. 8.7% is a tempting distractor close to 2021's growth of 8.68%, a different period. In practice: economists and treasury teams track such quarterly growth releases to update forecasts.

questions.q: Using Table 10.1 of the study material (GDP growth %, Economic Survey), compute the average growth for 1992–1996, 2008–2012 and 2017–2021. By how many percentage points did the 1992–1996 average exceed the Hindu growth rate? Which of the three periods was most affected by an external shock, and why?

model.text: 2017–2021 has the lowest average (3.81%) because of the pandemic contraction of about -6.6% in 2020; 2008–2012 was pulled down by the 2008 global financial crisis (about 3.09%).

remarks: Many add −6.6 as +6.6, overstating the 2017–21 average.
mistakes: Dividing by the wrong number of years.
Calling a difference between two rates a "per cent" change.
tips: List the five values before averaging; keep the sign of 2020.

questions.q: What were the causes of the 1991 economic crisis in India? State the objectives of the reforms and list the main measures of the New Industrial Policy, 1991.

model.text: Causes: (1) revenue expenditure persistently above revenue receipts through the 1980s, with large fiscal deficits financed by internal and external debt; (2) heavy public debt and interest burden; (3) the 1990 Gulf war raised oil prices and strained the balance of payments; (4) reserves fell to US$1.2 billion — about two weeks of imports; (5) import curbs reduced industrial output; (6) IMF loans came with strict conditions; (7) political instability caused a crisis of confidence.
Objectives: move from a centrally directed, controlled economy to a market-friendly one; and stabilise the economy by sharply cutting the fiscal deficit.

items: Public-sector reservation cut to 8 industries (now 2 — atomic energy, railway transport).
MRTP Act restructured — merger and takeover provisions removed, no pre-entry approval for expansion.
Automatic approval for FDI up to 51%.
Disinvestment of government equity in PSUs and greater autonomy to them.

scheme.pt: External causes (Gulf war, BoP, reserves US$1.2 bn ≈ two weeks)
At least four NIP measures with numbers (18/5, 8/2, 51%)

remarks: Marks are lost for vague answers ("there was a crisis") without the reserve figure.
mistakes: Mixing 1980s measures (broad-banding, MODVAT) into the 1991 list.
tips: Use three headings: Causes, Objectives, Measures.

questions.q: Using the figures in the study material, compute: (a) how far the average of Sixth and Seventh Plan growth (5.7% and 5.8%) exceeded the Hindu growth rate; (b) the multiple by which the MRTP asset limit rose in 1985-86 (₹20 crore → ₹100 crore); (c) the relative reduction in the top tariff from 355% (1990-91) to 50% (1995-96). State one reform each from the 1980s and from 1991 that these figures relate to.

model.text: 1980s: raising the MRTP threshold to ease constraints on large firms. 1991: phased tariff reduction under trade-policy reform.

scheme.pt: Links each figure to the right reform period
kw: 1980s mrtp|mrtp 1980|1985 mrtp|mrtp threshold|raising mrtp|raise mrtp|mrtp raised|mrtp relax|1980 mrtp
1991 tariff|tariff reduction|tariff cut|lower tariff|trade policy|trade reform|cut tariff|1991 trade

remarks: Good answers keep the 1980s and 1991 measures separate.
mistakes: Reporting (c) as 305% instead of a relative cut of about 86%.
tips: Write the formula in words first.

questions.q: Compare the Planning Commission and NITI Aayog on four points.

head: Basis
Planning Commission
NITI Aayog
rows: Think tank; co-operative federalism; bottom-up (village-level) planning
Enhanced voice and influence of states
No role in budgeting or expenditure control (a key criticism)

kw: think tank|co operative federalism|cooperative federalism|bottom up|village
enhanced|greater|more voice|increased|stronger|cooperative federalism|co operative federalism|more say|more role
no role|no financial|no power|not allocate|cannot allocate|no budget|lacks|without financial

remarks: Strong answers mention the exclusion from the budget process.
mistakes: Saying NITI Aayog prepares Five-Year Plans.

summary: Ancient India: largest economy (1st–17th c. AD), ⅓–¼ of world wealth; Arthashastra (Kautilya) — seven elements of the state.

British rule: EIC 1757–1858, Crown 1858–1947; discriminatory tariffs → de-industrialisation → pressure on land, zamindari, debt. Industry: cotton (9 mn spindles, 5th, 1930s), jute (largest), iron (1814; 8th in 1930); manufacturing ≈7% of NDP (1946).
1951: literacy just above 18%, life expectancy ≈32. Nehruvian planning; IPR 1948 & 1956; BoP crisis 1958; Hindu growth rate 3.5% (1950–80).
Droughts 1966–67 → Green Revolution. Banks nationalised 14 (1969) + 6 (1980); MRTP 1969; SSI reservation 1967; 1965–81 worst period.
1980s "reforms by stealth": delicensing 25 groups (1985), broad-banding, MRTP ₹20 → ₹100 crore, MODVAT, SEBI (12 April 1988), OGL 1,329 items, REER depreciation ~30%; growth 5.7% / 5.8%.

1991: reserves US$1.2 bn ≈ 2 weeks of imports; objectives — market orientation + stabilisation. viva.q: What is meant by the Hindu growth rate, and why was growth so slow?
viva.model: The Hindu growth rate refers to the modest average GDP growth of about 3.5 percent a year in the three decades from 1950 to 1980. Growth was slow because of the licence raj and heavy controls, an inward-looking closed economy, a dominant and inefficient public sector, restrictions like the MRTP Act and small-scale reservation, and shocks such as wars, droughts and oil price rises.

points.pt: About 3.5% average growth
Period 1950–1980 (first three decades)
Causes: licence raj/controls, closed economy, public-sector dominance, MRTP/SSI curbs, shocks

viva.q: What caused the economic crisis of 1991?
viva.model: In 1991 India faced huge fiscal deficits financed by internal and external debt, with heavy interest payments. Oil prices shot up because of the Gulf war, straining the balance of payments, and foreign exchange reserves fell to about 1.2 billion dollars, enough for only two weeks of imports. India had to borrow from the IMF on strict conditions, and political instability created a crisis of confidence.

points.pt: Large fiscal deficits, debt and interest burden
Gulf war oil price rise; balance-of-payments crisis
Reserves down to about US$1.2 billion — two weeks of imports
IMF conditions; crisis of confidence

viva.q: What were the main measures of the New Industrial Policy of 1991?
viva.model: The New Industrial Policy of July 1991 abolished industrial licensing except for eighteen industries, now only five. It cut the industries reserved for the public sector to eight, now just atomic energy and railway transport. It restructured the MRTP Act, removing prior approval for expansion and mergers, de-reserved many small-scale items, allowed automatic approval of foreign investment up to fifty-one percent and began disinvestment of public sector enterprises.

Public-sector reservation cut to 8 (now atomic energy and railways)
MRTP Act restructured; SSI de-reservation

viva.q: What is NITI Aayog and how is it different from the Planning Commission?
viva.model: NITI Aayog, the National Institution for Transforming India, replaced the Planning Commission on the first of January 2015. It works as a think tank of the government and promotes co-operative federalism by giving states a greater voice, with planning from the village level upwards. Unlike the Planning Commission, it does not allocate funds or take part in the budget process, which critics see as its main weakness.

viva.q: What was the Green Revolution and why was it needed?
viva.model: After two severe droughts in 1966 and 1967, India faced a food crisis and depended on American food aid under PL 480. The Green Revolution shifted farm policy from land reforms to raising productivity, especially of wheat, using high-yielding seed varieties with intensive irrigation, fertilisers and pesticides. It sharply increased food grain production and solved the food problem.

viva.q: Describe the role of the services sector in the Indian economy today.
viva.model: Services are India's largest sector, at about 53.89 percent of gross value added, and the fastest growing, with the highest labour productivity. India moved from agriculture straight to services, largely bypassing industry. Services lead in exports of software and business services and attract more than sixty percent of FDI equity inflows.

viva.q: What were the early reforms of the nineteen eighties?
viva.model: The reforms of the nineteen eighties, called reforms by stealth, included delicensing of twenty-five broad industry groups in 1985, broad-banding to let firms change their product mix, raising the MRTP asset limit from twenty crore to one hundred crore, introducing MODVAT, setting up SEBI in 1988, expanding the open general licence list and a realistic exchange rate. viva.q: How did British rule affect Indian industry and agriculture?
viva.model: Under British rule India was turned from an exporter of manufactured goods into an exporter of raw materials and a market for British machine-made goods. Discriminatory tariffs and cheap imports destroyed Indian handicrafts. Displaced artisans crowded into agriculture, causing fragmentation of holdings, subsistence farming and low productivity, while the zamindari system brought high rents, absentee landlords and heavy indebtedness.

cases.title: A minister's briefing note on three decades of reform
cases.case: A briefing note, using figures from the study material, says: "In 1991 our reserves were only US$1.2 billion. We cut the top tariff from 355% in 1990-91 to 85% by 1993-94 and devalued the rupee by about 18%. Licensing now applies to only five industries. Growth, which averaged 3.5% during 1950–80, reached about 8.85% in 1999 and, after a fall of about 6.6% in 2020, rebounded to about 8.68% in 2021. Public debt was about 86% of GDP in FY21/22. The Planning Commission was replaced on 1 January 2015."

mcqs.q: By how many percentage points did growth swing from 2020 to 2021, as per the note?
mcqs.explain: Swing = 2021 growth − 2020 growth = 8.68 − (−6.60) = 8.68 + 6.60 = 15.28 percentage points. The tempting 2.08 forgets that 2020 growth was negative (8.68 − 6.60); 8.68 and 6.6 are the individual figures. In practice: analysts describe such swings as 'base effects', since a rebound after a sharp fall can look very large.

mcqs.q: The relative fall in the top tariff from 355% to 85% is approximately:
mcqs.explain: Relative fall = (355 − 85) ÷ 355 × 100 = 270 ÷ 355 × 100 ≈ 76.06%. The tempting 270% is the fall in percentage points, not a relative percentage; 23.94% is the new rate as a share of the old (85 ÷ 355); 85% is the new rate itself. In practice: precise language — percentage points versus percent — matters when CAs and economists write budget commentaries.

mcqs.q: Which of the following still requires an industrial licence, as per the material?
mcqs.explain: Per the material, five industries still need a licence — arms and ammunition; atomic substances; narcotics and hazardous chemicals; alcoholic drinks; and cigarettes and cigars. Narcotic drugs and hazardous chemicals are on the list. Automobiles, steel and cement are traps — all were delicensed after 1991. In practice: new projects in chemical and pharmaceutical manufacturing must check whether they handle licensed hazardous substances.

mcqs.q: The body that replaced the Planning Commission is mainly criticised for:
options: Having no role in the budget process
mcqs.explain: The body that replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015 is NITI Aayog. Its main criticism is that it has no role in the budget process and so cannot direct resources the way the Planning Commission did. 'Controlling state budgets' is the trap — it has no such power. In practice: NITI Aayog influences policy mainly through research, indices and advice to ministries and States.
mcqs.topic: NITI Aayog: a Bold Step for Transforming India

mcqs.q: The debt figure in the note compares with the EMDE average (IMF, 2022) of:
mcqs.explain: Per the material, the EMDE average debt in 2022 (IMF) was 64.5% of GDP, against India's 86% in FY21/22. The tempting 86% is India's own figure; 46% is a distractor. In practice: sovereign-rating analysts compare India's debt with peer averages like this, and the gap is a key reason for India's fiscal-consolidation targets.
